enrichment.short_title: Health and Safety fine reduction after roofer fell through roof light

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Self-employed roof sheeter Simon Pickering fell through an uncovered roof light at commercial premises in York on 25 May 2000 and died from his injuries.

Yorkshire Sheeting and Insulation Ltd, specialist roofing subcontractor, pleaded guilty with main contractor Totty Building Services Ltd to section 3(1) breaches after incomplete safety netting and uncovered roof lights near the working area.
The Crown Court fined the appellant £100,000 plus costs; Totty was fined £10,000.
Safety nets had been delayed by vandalism; some instructions had been given to confine work to netted bays but demarcation was inadequate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) by leave of the single judge after guilty pleas committed from the magistrates' court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; fine reduced from £100,000 to £55,000; costs order unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: A sentencing judge must assess the defendant's own culpability for the charged offence rather than apportion overall moral blame between corporate defendants by percentage; where the only aggravating factor beyond death is the fatality itself and strong mitigating features are present, a fine of £100,000 was manifestly excessive for this reputable company's serious but short-lived default.
legal_issues: Whether the sentencing judge erred in treating the deceased as the appellant's employee rather than an independent contractor's ganger
Whether apportioning 90% culpability to the roofing subcontractor distorted assessment of the appellant's criminal default
Appropriate fine level for section 3(1) Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 breach causing death
index_terms: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

confidence.notes: Outcome, ratio on sentencing approach, and statutory basis are explicit; fine quantum involves conventional appellate assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Purchaser indemnity for Marpaul building contract claims
key_facts: Lomax Leisure Ltd entered administration and sold nightclub development assets to Fabric London Ltd under an asset sale agreement dated 13 May 1999.
The building contract with Marpaul had been terminated for insolvency before the sale, but arbitration awards left net liability and substantial defence costs against the company.
The purchaser took the benefit of completed works and relief against forfeiture of the lease; contracts were nominally priced at £2.
Clause 8.1 required the purchaser to indemnify the vendor against claims, costs, and proceedings in respect of the contracts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: CPR Part 24 application for declarations as to indemnity liability only; quantum to be determined separately.
enrichment.outcome: Company entitled to indemnity under clause 8.1 for Marpaul's primary liability and costs solely attributable to defending Marpaul's claim, but not for counterclaim costs used as set-off.
enrichment.ratio: A terminated building contract's outstanding netting and damages obligations remained 'contracts' within the agreement; the purchaser assumed burden as well as benefit and clause 8.1 indemnified the vendor for claims made against it by Marpaul, but counterclaim pursuit was the vendor's own cost under clause 8.6.
legal_issues: Construction of 'Contracts' definition where the building contract had been terminated before transfer
Scope of clause 8.1 indemnity for arbitration awards and defence costs
Whether counterclaim costs fell within indemnity or vendor's own expense under clause 8.6
linked_authorities: Rat Holdings Limited administration case [1999] 3 All ER 22

confidence.notes: Declaratory outcome and clause construction are clearly reasoned; quantum and some cost allocation remain for later determination.

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurance disclosure and unfounded moral hazard allegations
key_facts: Reinsurers subscribed to primary and excess layers of reinsurance of a Colombian bank's blanket bond and professional indemnity cover in 1997–1999.
They avoided the contracts alleging non-disclosure of press and media allegations of impropriety against the bank president Mr Medina and senior officers.
The defendants sought to prove at trial that the allegations were unfounded to argue they were not material.
The claimants applied to debar evidence that allegations were without foundation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Restored case management conference on whether defendants could rely on subsequent proof that allegations against Mr Medina were unfounded.
enrichment.outcome: Paragraph 5(1) of the amended defence struck out; defendants debarred from adducing evidence that allegations and charges were unfounded.
enrichment.ratio: Materiality of circumstances for disclosure must be judged at the time of placing by reference to information available to the underwriter; reports, rumours, or allegations that would influence a prudent insurer do not cease to be material because they are later shown to have been false, including allegations relevant to moral hazard.
legal_issues: Whether subsequent proof that allegations were unfounded renders them immaterial for non-disclosure
Whether moral hazard allegations must be disclosed even if unfounded at time of placing
Appropriate case management where striking out achieves same effect as debarring evidence
index_terms: Caja de Credito Agraria Industrial y Minero
linked_authorities: March Cabaret Club & Casino Ltd v The London Assurance
Reynolds v Phoenix Assurance Co Ltd
Inversiones Manria S.A. v Sphere Drake Insurance Co Plc (The Dora)
Gate v Sun Alliance Insurance Ltd
Strive Shipping Corporation v Hellenic Mutual War Risks Association (The Grecia Express)
Drake Insurance Plc v Provident Insurance Plc

confidence.notes: Clear interlocutory ruling on materiality with extensive authority review; full trial issues on misrepresentation remain outstanding.

enrichment.short_title: Long service award pension enhancement after thirty years' payment
key_facts: Miss Watts received a long service award in 1969 increasing her pension by £16.50 per month; the enhanced pension was paid continuously for nearly thirty years until February 2000.
The council withdrew the enhancement after advice that past LSAs and resulting pension increases might be ultra vires.
The Pensions Ombudsman reinstated the enhancement with arrears, interest, and £250 for maladministration.
The council appealed on law only, challenging lawfulness of the award and the maladministration finding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court (Chancery Division) from a Pensions Ombudsman determination on a point of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; maladministration compensation quashed; principal pension reinstatement decision upheld and appeal dismissed on lawfulness.
enrichment.ratio: A long-promised council LSA policy inducing retention of experienced staff may be intra vires unlike a one-off salary inflation at departure; once an enhanced pension was paid without challenge for nearly thirty years the evidential burden shifted to the council to prove the original award was ultra vires, and the Ombudsman's finding of individual merit-based award was not perverse.
legal_issues: Whether general LSA policy enhancing pensions was ultra vires local authority pay-fixing powers
Evidential burden where pension enhancement paid for decades without challenge
Whether Ombudsman erred in finding maladministration in withdrawing enhancement
Jurisdiction of Pensions Ombudsman to decide questions of pension law
index_terms: London Borough of Barking and Dagenham
linked_authorities: Legal & General Insurance v Pensions Ombudsman

confidence.notes: Principal pension point and split appeal outcome are clear; historical policy lawfulness involves fact-sensitive local government analysis.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC murder reference after midnight shooting at gravel pits
key_facts: In June 1990 the appellant fired a pistol at a departing car near flooded gravel pits, killing an 18-year-old girl in the back seat; he was convicted of murder in 1991 and sentenced to detention for life.
The defence at trial was that he aimed to miss and lacked intent for murder; he had not given evidence and relied on interview accounts and firearms expert evidence.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case on fresh expert evidence (Dr Renshaw) on bullet drop and possible firing distance, and alleged summing-up deficiencies.
Witness evidence placed the car within a short distance when shot, not at the 185-yard scenario Dr Renshaw suggested.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) following CCRC reference after dismissal of first appeal in 1991.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe; fresh evidence not received.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh expert evidence on an alternative long-distance firing scenario could not satisfy section 23 where all witness evidence indicated the car was within 50 yards and the appellant's own account was that he fired downward; deficiencies in summing up the defence did not render the conviction unsafe where the jury's issue was a simple question of intention at the time of firing.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Renshaw's fresh evidence met Criminal Appeal Act 1968 section 23 criteria
Whether the trial judge failed adequately to identify and summarise the defence case to the jury
Whether firearms trajectory evidence undermined proof of intent for murder

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome and grounds analysis are detailed; underlying factual dispute on intent was resolved at original trial.

enrichment.short_title: National minimum wage for live-in domiciliary carer
key_facts: Miss Walton was a live-in carer for an epileptic client, paid £31.40 per day for three days on and four off, with free accommodation and meals.
She was required to remain on premises but rarely disturbed at night; Inland Revenue assessment with her agreement recorded 6 hours 50 minutes average daily task time.
Dividing pay by 24 hours yielded below minimum wage; dividing by 6 hours 50 minutes exceeded it.
Employment Tribunal and EAT held she performed unmeasured work, not time work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissing national minimum wage claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; national minimum wage satisfied using daily average agreement under regulation 28.
enrichment.ratio: A worker paid by broad assessment of task difficulty and duration rather than by reference to time worked performs unmeasured work under regulation 6, not time work under regulation 3(a); a realistic written daily average agreement under regulation 28 validly determines hours for minimum wage calculation and does not treat all on-premises sleeping time as working time.
legal_issues: Whether live-in carer work was time work or unmeasured work under regulation 3
Whether regulation 28 daily average agreement applied to hours calculation
Distinction between payment by time as unit of account and payment by reference to time worked
index_terms: British Nursing Association v Inland Revenue
linked_authorities: British Nursing Association v Inland Revenue

confidence.notes: Statutory classification and regulatory construction are central and clearly resolved; Low Pay Commission policy context noted but not dispositive.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 removal disproportionate after asylum delay
key_facts: Ethnic Albanian from Kosovo claimed asylum on arrival in June 1997; no decision for over four years while he had temporary admission.
During that period he formed a lasting relationship with a Czech refugee and her two sons, whom he married in October 2001.
The adjudicator found family life in the UK could not realistically be enjoyed in Kosovo; removal would interfere with Article 8 rights.
The IAT equated the appellant with an ordinary out-of-country spouse applicant, ignoring Home Office delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive appeal to the Court of Appeal after permission granted on adjourned application from Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision under section 65.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the Secretary of State; removal held disproportionate breach of Article 8.
enrichment.ratio: Where Home Office delay over four years meant the appellant would likely have obtained leave to remain as a Kosovo refugee and could have applied in-country to vary leave on marriage, treating him as a standard out-of-country spouse applicant ignores an exceptional circumstance that renders removal disproportionate under Article 8 despite immigration control objectives.
legal_issues: Proportionality of removal interfering with established family life under Article 8(2)
Effect of Secretary of State delay in processing asylum claim on immigration policy application
Whether appellant should be treated as ordinary spouse seeking entry clearance from abroad
linked_authorities: R (Mahmood) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
Secretary of State for the Home Department v Isiko
International Transport Roth GmbH v Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Article 8 outcome and delay rationale are clearly articulated; asylum risk findings were overtaken by events but human rights ground was decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Resuming father contact despite Schedule 1 offender history
key_facts: Father with Schedule 1 convictions for sexual offences against girls sought contact with his 10-year-old daughter C living with the mother.
Over 60 court orders since 1997; contact had been fortnightly in summer 2002 until mother stopped it in August over minor incidents.
CAFCASS recommended monthly contact escalating to fortnightly; mother did not attend the February 2003 hearing.
The case was part-heard with a parallel immunisation dispute adjourned for psychiatric evidence on the mother.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part-heard applications for specific issue orders on contact and immunisation in Portsmouth family proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Contact ordered to resume monthly for up to two months then fortnightly; penal notice available on written application if contact fails.
enrichment.ratio: Where long-delayed contact had been proceeding adequately, minor incidents did not justify cessation; a child of ten expressing clear wishes through CAFCASS, supported by acquittal on a related burglary count and psychiatric evidence on the mother's difficulties, warranted resuming structured contact without immediate penal notice while therapeutic exploration with the mother continued.
legal_issues: Whether mother had sufficient justification to stop contact in August 2002
Weight to be given to child's wishes for contact with Schedule 1 offender father
Appropriate contact frequency and enforcement without counter-productive penal notice

confidence.notes: Contact outcome and reasoning are clear from February 2003 judgment; immunisation application was adjourned and not finally decided in this judgment.

enrichment.short_title: No occupiers' duty to mid-winter harbour trespasser diver
key_facts: Professional diver Mr Donoghue dived from a harbour slipway shortly after midnight on 27 December 1997, struck submerged grid piles, and became tetraplegic.
Folkestone Properties knew children swam and dived from the slipway in summer but prohibited swimming; grid piles stood 80cm proud of the harbour bed.
The judge held a summer duty existed and a warning sign would have dissuaded the diver; contributory negligence reduced damages to 25%.
No reasonable grounds existed to believe anyone would swim or dive in mid-winter at night.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from High Court judgment upholding liability under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim dismissed; no duty owed at time of accident.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 1(3)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 the test whether a trespasser may come into the vicinity of a danger must be applied to the circumstances at the actual time and place of injury; knowledge that trespassers might swim in summer does not impose a winter midnight duty to a professional diver where no reasonable grounds existed to anticipate presence near submerged grid piles.
legal_issues: Whether section 1(3) duty is owed to a class of trespassers irrespective of season and time
Application of section 1(3)(b) at actual time and place of accident
Whether Tomlinson v Congleton required duty analysis without regard to individual circumstances
Whether warning sign obligation persists when no trespassers reasonably expected
linked_authorities: White v The Council of the City and District of St Albans
Robert Addie and Sons (Collieries) Ltd v Dumbreck

confidence.notes: Appellate ratio on section 1(3)(b) timing is explicit and fully reasoned; first-instance liability findings were overturned.

enrichment.short_title: Aggravated burglary conviction unsafe after duress misdirection
key_facts: The appellant admitted aggravated burglary at Mr W's home on 24 January 2000 but claimed duress by X, associated with an escort agency operator, who allegedly murdered a man and stored the body in a car boot.
A confidential off-the-record police interview about X's murder admissions was later used to challenge the timing of duress threats.
The judge misdirected on duress questions three and four regarding escape and voluntary association.
The jury acquitted on a prior count relating to the same premises in August 1999.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction for aggravated burglary and sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe; sentence appeal fell away; reporting restrictions on confidential police material.
enrichment.ratio: A confidential police statement used to undermine a duress defence is a confession under PACE section 76 when ultimately self-incriminating in context and obtained after a confidentiality assurance likely to render it unreliable; combined with misdirections on whether the accused could avoid duress by pretence and on voluntary association without requiring anticipation of pressure to commit the type of crime charged, the conviction was unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether confidential off-the-record police interview was admissible under section 76 or section 78 PACE
Whether Saunders v UK requires widening the definition of confession in section 82(1)
Correct formulation of duress questions on avoiding threats and voluntary association
Whether association with criminals must involve foresight of pressure to commit the type of offence charged
linked_authorities: R v Croydon Justices ex parte Dean
Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland v Lynch

confidence.notes: Quashed conviction and legal grounds are comprehensively analysed; underlying truth of duress narrative was contested at trial.
